body: For petitioner(s): Mr. Younas Ali Shah, advocate.
For respondent(s): Mr. Yasir Rauf Wazir, advocate.

*****+* SABITALI.AE KHAN,J,l. This civil revision petition under section ll5 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 ('C.P.C.") assails the judgment and decree dated 16.10.2024 of the leamed Additional District Judge-V, Bannu, dismissing Civil Appeal No. 199/13 of 2024. That judgment affirmed the order dated lO.Ol.2O24 of the learned Civil Judge-X, Bannu, rejecting the plaint in Civil Suit No. 27ll of 2023 under Order MI' Rule 11, C.P.C. On21.03.2023,the petitioner sued respondent No. l, the then S.H.O, and respondent No' 2, the District Police offrcer, Bannu, for damages for malicious prosecution. He pleaded that respondent No. l, with mala fide intent, implicated him in case FIR No. 10 dated 16.10.2019, registered under sections 124,353, 148 and 149, P.P.C, at Police Station Sub-Division Wazir, Bannu' He further pleadedthathewasarrestedandtortured,andthataftersubmissionofthe challan he was discharged by the leamed Additional sessions Judge-I, Barrnu, on 13.|l'202|. Both Courts below held that a discharge, unlike an acquittal, fumishes no foundation for the action. The appellate court added that mala fide could not be inferred in the absence of evidence and of an order of acquittal.

2. Leamed counsel for the petitioner contended that the petitioner was non-suited without issues being framed or evidence recorded. He argued that malice and want ofreasonable and probable cause are questions offact, and that a discharge on the prosecution's own application was a termination in the petitioner's favour. Learned counsel for the respondents supported the impugned decisions. Two questions therefore arise. The first is whether a discharge, by its very nature, disentitles a plaintiff from suing for malicious prosecution. The second, which goes to the root of the matter, is whether the suit was within time. Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908 obliges the Court to examine the second question suo motu, whether or not the parties raised it.

3. Under Order VII, Rule I l, C.P.C., the plaint is read meaningfully and as a whole, together with the documents on which it relies. The Court does not try disputed facts or decide the case on the defence pleas (Iewan and 7 olhers v. Federation of Pakistan, f994 SCMR E26). The rule does not, however, require the Court to accept every averment as gospel truth, and the Court retains its inherent power to see through a plaint that is barred on its own showing. Where such a bar is apparent, the Court must reject the plaint at the outset rather than permit a futile trial (Haji Abdul Karim and others v. Messrs Florida Builders (Pvt.) Ltd., PLD 2012 SC 247); (Mst, Rehmat Begam v. Mehfooz Ahmed and others, PLD 2024 SC 1f08). Section 2(2), C.P.C, deems the rejection of a plaint to be a decree. The kial Court's omission to draw up a decree-sheet was therefore a curable ( irregularity, which affected neither the competence of the appeal nor the validity of the proceedings.

4. The action for malicious prosecution lies only where the following ingredients coexist: prosecution of the plaintiff by the defendant; its termination in the plaintiffs favour; want of reasonable and probable cause; malice; interference with the plaintiffs liberty or reputation; and resulting damage (Muhammad Aktam v. Mst. Farman Bi, PLD 1990 SC 28)' The tort rests on abuse of the process of law, and the failure of a prosecution does not by itself make its initiation malicious (Niaz and others v' Abdul Saflar and olhers,PLD 2006 SC 432)' Even proofofwant ofreasonable and probable cause is not, in itself' proof of malice' which must be independently established (Muhammad Yousaf v' Abdul Qayyum' PLD 2016 SC 478). The same principle has been applied by the High Courts' whichhaveheldthatthelawraisesnopresumptionthateveryprosecution ending in acquittal was malicious [Laal Zaman v' Farhad Ali' 2023 MLD 1920; PIJ 2025 Lahore 346 (DB)l' 5. A discharge is not an acquittal after trial' Its effect depends on the provision under which it was passed and the circumstances in which it was made. In Subedar (Retd')

Fazale Rahimv' Rab Nawaz(1999 SCMR 700)' a discharge under section 16g, cr.p.c, even when coupled with proceedings against the complainant under section 182' P'P'C' left the plaintiff burdened with proving want of reasonable cause and malice' lt Abdul Rauf v' Abdul Rauak(PLD 1994 SC 476)' the claim failed despite a discharge because a potice challan had shown reasonable cause (see also Sultan alias Kaloo v' Haji Muhammad Khan'2015 CLC 150)' At the same time' Article 23 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908 speaks of a plaintiffwho "is acquitted, or the prosecution is otherwise terminated." These words show that acquittal is not the only favourable termination known to law' A discharge is thus neither a bar to the action nor proof of its ingredients' 6. In the present case, the discharge was ordered by a Court after the challan had been submitted. It was made on the prosecution's own ' application under section 4-C(ii) read with section 5(B) of the Khyber PakhfunkhwaProsecutionService(Constitution,FunctionsarrdPowers) Act, 2005, read with sections 63,265-D and 494, Cr'P'C, and the Court recorded that nothing existed on file beyond the bald allegations of the crimereport.TheCourtsbelowthereforemisdirectedthemselvesinheating the discharge as a bar in itself. The appellate court further erred in faulting thepetitionerforawantofevidencethathewasneverallowedtoproduce' relying on LaalZanan (supra) and Noor Ali v' Ptovince of Sindh (PLD 2020Karachi700),bothofwhichweredecidedonevidencerecordedat trial. This misdirection, however, does not avail the petitioner' because the plaint founders on an independent statutory bar' 7. Article 23 requires a suit for malicious prosecution to be brought within one year of the termination of the prosecution' Time runs from that termination, and later proceedings do not extend it' The petitioner's own case rests on the discharge of 13.11.2021. Excluding the day of accrual under section l2(l) of the Act, limitation expired onl3'll'2022' whereas the suit was filed ot21.03.2023, four months and eight days late' order MI, Rule 6, C.P.C. requires a time-barred plaint to state the ground of exemption. This plaint states none, its annexures disclose none' and section 5 of the Act does not apply to suits. Where the relevant dates are admitted on the face of the plaint, limitation is a pure question of law. Section 3 then mandates dismissal although limitation was not pleaded, and the expression "barred by any law" in Order VII, Rule ll(d), C.p.C. embraces the Limitation Act. A correct conclusion is not disturbed merely because it was reached for a different reason, and remanding a suit that is barred on its own showing would only prolong futile litigation.

8. The jurisdiction under section 115, C.P.C. is supervisory and discretionary, and it is not a second appeal. It is attracted only where a subordinate Court has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested, or acted illegally or with material irregularity, and no such defect affects the result reached here. This decision rests solely on limitation. It is not a finding on the allegations of malicious prosecution or torhrre, on the respondents' conduct, or on the petitioner's entitlement to damages on merits. Consequently, this civil revision petition is dismissed.
